name: MARPE (mini-implant palate expander)

card.summary: A palate expander anchored to the palatal bone with mini-screws so it can widen the upper jaw in teens and young adults without cutting the bone; studies show skeletal widening, but cosmetic effects are barely studied.
card.aka: Microimplant-assisted rapid palatal expansion, miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion, MSE (a specific four-screw design)
card.note: Evidence is for transverse maxillary deficiency (bite and airway); effects on facial aesthetics are not well established, and expansion amounts vary with age and suture maturity.

quick.overview:
MARPE is an orthodontic appliance that widens a narrow upper jaw. It resembles a conventional rapid palatal expander, but is fixed to the roof of the mouth with small bone screws instead of relying only on the teeth. This is intended to push the two halves of the palate apart rather than tipping the teeth outward.

In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as a core non-surgical 'hardmaxx' tool for a narrow palate, with users discussing cheekbone width, midface support and breathing. Published research focuses on bite correction and skeletal change on CBCT scans, not on attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Two to four mini-implants engage the palatal bone and the expander screw is turned to separate the midpalatal suture. Because the force is delivered to bone, proponents say more of the change is skeletal, and a meta-analysis and CBCT studies of late adolescents and young adults report skeletal expansion along with some dental change.
quick.risks: Reported issues include incomplete suture opening in some patients, tooth tipping, pain, soreness, screw loosening or failure and expansion that is greater at the front of the palate than the back. It is a prescription orthodontic procedure; users on forums report costs in the thousands of dollars. Studies of long-term stability and facial appearance are limited.

lead: MARPE (micro-implant or miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion) is an orthodontic technique for widening the upper jaw in patients whose midpalatal suture is no longer easily opened by a conventional tooth-borne expander. The appliance is anchored to the palate with mini-implants and is used to treat maxillary transverse deficiency, a narrow upper jaw associated with crossbite, crowding and, in some patients, nasal airway restriction [1][4].

Clinical reports describe it as a non-surgical option for adults and late adolescents, as an alternative to surgically assisted expansion [1][4]. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis examined its efficacy in late adolescents and adults [6], and a randomized trial compared conventional expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT [10]. A named variant, the Maxillary Skeletal Expander (MSE), uses four bicortical mini-implants [3].

In looksmaxxing culture MARPE is discussed as a way to widen the maxilla and, proponents say, improve midface width and breathing [18][20]. The published literature addresses skeletal and dental outcomes; a trial of three-dimensional facial soft tissue changes and perceived appearance after MARPE is registered but not yet recruiting [16].

paras: A conventional rapid palatal expander is attached to the upper molars and works well in children, where the midpalatal suture is still open. In older patients, researchers note that expansion forces transmitted through the teeth can produce unwanted dental effects rather than true skeletal expansion, which prompted the development of mini-implant-supported designs [4][9].

In MARPE, mini-implants are placed in the palate and connected to the appliance, so that force is applied directly to bone. Finite element analyses have modelled how stress is distributed through the nasomaxillary complex with such appliances [2][8].

A case report describes a 19-year-old patient with maxillary constriction treated with a MARPE appliance and reports orthopedic correction of the deficiency [4]. A clinical article from 2017 describes non-surgical treatment of transverse deficiency in adults using MARPE [1].

Imaging studies of the MSE appliance in CBCT scans examined changes in the midpalatal and pterygopalatine sutures [3], and a CBCT study of young adults reported skeletal and dentoalveolar changes after miniscrew-assisted expansion [5]. A separate study examined the stability of these changes after treatment [7].

A prospective randomized clinical trial compared conventional rapid palatal expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT [10]. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in late adolescents and adults assessed its efficacy [6].

Registered trials include studies of MARPE with and without corticopuncture [12][15], of two versus four mini-screws in non-growing patients [13][14], of speech effects [17], of sleep and airway [11], and of three-dimensional facial soft tissue changes and perceived appearance [16].

The published evidence concerns correction of a narrow maxilla and the proportion of skeletal versus dental change. Reviewers describe a pursuit of 'pure orthopedic movement' as a goal that is approached but not always reached [9]. Patients' age and suture maturity are among the factors discussed in the literature [1][6].
No published trial in the sources reviewed here has established that MARPE changes facial attractiveness; the registered soft-tissue study [16] has not yet reported.

Users on looksmax.org discuss MARPE as a hardmaxx intervention, often in connection with palate width, cheekbone projection and breathing [18][20]. Some posters report their orthodontist's predicted expansion (for example about 6 mm for a teenager) and debate whether this is enough to justify the cost [20].

Threads also discuss whether widening could be unflattering for people who already have wide faces [19][25], how to obtain it, and combinations with facemask treatment or surgery [21][22][24]. These accounts are anecdotal.

timeline.event: A finite element study analyses stress distribution with micro-implant-assisted palatal expansion [2].
A case report describes MARPE correcting transverse maxillary deficiency in an adult [4].
CBCT studies report skeletal and dentoalveolar changes and suture changes with MARPE and MSE [3][5].
A systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in late adolescents and adults is published [6].
A randomized trial compares conventional expansion with MARPE [10].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org MARPE is a frequent topic among users interested in midface width, a 'narrow' palate and non-surgical alternatives to jaw surgery [18][20].

claims.claim: MARPE widens the cheekbones and midface
claims.believers: Posters report visible changes in cheek width after a few millimetres of expansion and describe the result as a facial improvement [18].
claims.experts: Published studies measure palatal and skeletal width on CBCT [5][10]; no published study has yet established effects on cheekbone appearance, though one on soft tissue is registered [16].

claims.claim: MARPE gives more skeletal and less dental change than a conventional expander
claims.believers: Forum users cite orthodontists who describe it as bone-anchored and suited to older patients [20].
claims.experts: A randomized trial compared the two approaches [10] and a meta-analysis reviewed MARPE in older patients [6]; investigators describe the approach as aiming to reduce dental side effects [4][9].

claims.claim: Expansion can make an already wide face look worse
claims.believers: Users with wide midfaces ask whether they should skip it or pair it with other procedures, and some warn it can change the look of the face [19][25].
claims.experts: No published studies have evaluated aesthetic outcomes by baseline facial width.

claims.claim: MARPE is worth it even for small expansions such as 4 to 6 mm
claims.believers: Threads debate whether a few millimetres is meaningful for looks, with some saying larger targets are preferable [20][23][26].
claims.experts: Published work reports millimetre-scale expansion measured on imaging [5][7]; clinicians frame the goal as correcting the transverse deficiency.
